<reason>Both sides argued with real sophistication, but A stayed truer to the proposition as written. A's core mechanism—redemption promises can outrun accessible reserves, creating run risk analogous to banks/MMFs—was consistent from opening to close, and A correctly held B accountable to the motion's "more like" (not "identical to") standard. B's "third box" strategy was clever and its pressure questions (forcing A to specify which concrete tools survive) genuinely stressed A's case, and B's "escrow agents are bank-like too" reductio was a sharp moment. But B's final position—conceding an enforceable, supervisor-enforced, stress-tested liquidity floor while insisting this is merely "custody/trust law" rather than fund-like regulation—reads as a semantic retreat rather than a substantive rebuttal, since forward-looking liquidity requirements calibrated to redemption stress are a hallmark of prudential financial regulation, not ordinary bailment law. A's closing correctly exploited this: B "accepted the constraint and disputed only the label." B's opening was also clipped by the word limit, costing it some foundational development. On balance, A gave the cleaner, more decision-relevant answer to the motion as framed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Rebuttal 2 exchange where B concedes (A2 answer) it would support an enforceable minimum liquid-reserve requirement, and A's Closing reframes that concession as proof CON accepted bank/MMF-style substance while merely contesting the label—this was the pivotal, debate-deciding clash.</best_rebuttal>
